utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Let me first try to adjust my seat. Mr. Ierace, yesterday you indicated you would like to have -- to make some observation as far as, well, should I say the scope of cross-examination is concerned. I'd like to do that just before the first break we'll have, and I think that both parties should have five minutes to explain their views. So we'll do that just before half past 10.00. That would mean, unless there are any other messages, that we could now start the examination-in-chief of Mr. Kucanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is correct, and I must apologise for what happened yesterday afternoon. That was the fault of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Kucanin's name was left off the witness list for yesterday. That list was provided to the Victims and Witnesses Unit on Monday afternoon. It was an oversight by a team member, and again, I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your apologies are accepted. Then, Mr. Usher, I think you could bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, before we bring in the expert, I should like to thank the Chamber for the problems -- I should like to apologise for the problems that I caused yesterday. I have to say that the Defence, it seems, has not to date received the tape, the arrival of which was announced yesterday. We still do not have the tape, and I wanted to indicate that issue to you right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, firstly, there was no interpretation of the French, but I have, of course, the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- of what Mr. Piletta-Zanin said. I'll make some inquiries at the first break to find out if we have a copy ready to hand over to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kucanin, can you hear me in a language you understand? Yes. Mr. Kucanin, first of all, welcome in this courtroom. Before you give your testimony in this courtroom, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. Mr. Kucanin, the order is that you'll first be examined by the counsel for the Prosecution. You'll then be examined by counsel for the Defence, and whenever the Judges have any additional questions, you'll hear from them. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is your name Mirsad Kucanin?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Mirsad Kucanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: During 1992, did you live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you a member of the police force?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note that I don't have a translation through the headphones from Bosnian to English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: My apologies. It's my mistake. I'm on the wrong channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When did you join the police force? In what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: By 1992, were you a criminal inspector in the centre of the Security Service in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was the centre of the Security Service sometimes known as the CSB?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As an inspector, did your responsibilities include the investigation of serious crimes, including homicides and sexual crimes, for the whole district of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did those responsibilities continue throughout the conflict, that is, between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At the beginning of the armed conflict, did the police service have a number of departments, including a Criminal Investigation Department, a Criminal Technical Department, a Criminal Analytical Department, and Aliens Department, a Uniform Department, and a Special Department?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes, more or less that would have been the main departments of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Immediately before the outbreak of the armed conflict, were there ten police stations in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Following the outbreak of hostilities, were those ten police stations divided between the two primary sides to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Since there were ten municipalities within the town, there were ten stations for public security. When the war broke out, six of them remained under the control of the Bosnian Serbs, whereas four public security stations remained under the control of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were the four that remained under the control of Bosnia and Herzegovina Centar, Novi Grad, Novo Sarajevo, and Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kucanin, the interpreters have some difficulties in hearing you, so we first try to get the microphones a bit closer to you. And would you please speak clearly and loud enough for the interpreters to hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were the six that came under the control of the Bosnian Serbs Pale, Ilidza, Trnovo, Hadzici, Ilijas, and Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Approximately how many police officers were there following the division of the police stations operating in the area controlled by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Do you mean in total, within the police, or how many policemen in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How many policemen were left to operate the four police stations?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: As for the uniformed police, there could have been about a hundred police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And how many investigators or inspectors were there of those 100? I withdraw that question. How many investigators or inspectors were there?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: At the beginning there were very few of us left, maybe up to 15. I am talking about the centre of the Security Service. There may have been two or three other police officers within those four police stations, but we were forced to call back in service the reserve force, or people who had similar educational backgrounds, so that they would also be engaged. So the final number was about 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Did the police service in Sarajevo, before the war, come under the control of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did it remain under the control of the Ministry of the Interior throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were forced to call back into service the reserve force. Did the reserve force come under the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: During the armed conflict, at one point did some of the reserve police come -- assume military duties?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes, those though I cannot remember the exact year or the date, but I remember that an order came, since the police was the only disciplined body on the territory which was under the control of the BH government, that is, which was not occupied, a request was made to reactivate the reserve police force for the defence of Sarajevo. I'm only talking about the reserve force now. So that is how a certain number of reserve police officers came under this control.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Before the war, did the regular members of the police service have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: During the war and throughout the war, did the regular members of the police service have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: The majority did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What about the reserve police members? Did they have uniforms during the war?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Not at the beginning. Occasionally someone got the upper part or the trousers or some other part of clothing, which indicated that they were members of the police, but they did not have a complete uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You said that a certain number of reserve police officers became involved in the defence of Sarajevo. At any stage, did the regular police officers become involved in the defence of the city?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes. In certain cases, specific cases, where intervention was required, where a certain area was exposed to danger, they provided us with support when we had to carry out our duties, and they went to those portions of the front or the area where defence was needed or where it was necessary to repel an enemy attack or similar situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You said just then that when a certain area was exposed to danger, they provided us with support when we had to carry out our duties. Do you mean by that that when you were carrying out your investigative duties in an area that was exposed, that you would receive some protection from other members of the regular police force?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: When we had to identify the perpetrator of an incident or perform a search or prevent black market activity, we had the support of them, that is, the people who were able to protect us while we were carrying out our regular police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You also said that the regular members of the police force, or at least some members, went to the portions of the front when it was necessary to repel an enemy attack or similar situation. How many times did that happen during the armed conflict between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the exact number of such cases, but certain areas of the town came under infantry attacks on almost a daily basis, and it was impossible to have the regular type of defence. So when some areas were physically threatened by the enemy, either from the infantry forces or armoured vehicles or other such equipment, when our defence lines were under imminent danger, then the police force would offer help if it was necessary to defend the specific area. So that is what they did in terms of defence during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When do you recollect the armed conflict commenced? In what month? In what year?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: The armed conflict --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure, but I'm listening to the Serb version. I think that the witness spoke about a considerable number of such attacks, which is not clear from the English text. Let me give you the reference. Page 8, line 20. More or less, I'm telling you this right away, also in view of the tape that we have to listen to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please invite the witness to clarify the issue, Mr. Ierace, whether there's any misunderstanding as far as page 8, line 20, is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President, but I do note page 8, lines 13 and 14 of the English translation, which seem to correspond with what Mr. Piletta-Zanin has referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps let me first ask Mr. Piletta-Zanin: It's not what we find in page 8, line 14, where the answer of the witness was that it was infantry attacks on almost a daily basis, which of course is a considerable frequency, I would even say. Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, more or less, but I think that the witness mentioned a very large number of attacks, which would imply a large number of reactions by the police. That is why I thought the precision was important. But the idea is the same, more or less. The witness, however, spoke about a high number of attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, if we talk about the -- he talked about attacks on a daily basis, and of course the implications, you could ask the witness about during cross-examination. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In what month of what year did the armed conflict commence in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: At the beginning of April 1992. To be more precise, in my view, it started on the 5th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You said that there were attacks on a daily basis. Did that apply throughout the period of the armed conflict, that there were attacks on a daily basis, or did it apply to some times -- some periods of time in particular?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Every day. During those four years, I don't remember one single day that Sarajevo didn't come under some form of attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but does that mean that regular members of the police service were involved in fighting every day during the armed conflict from 1992 through to 1995?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: No. I also understand the objection made by the Defence. The attacks were on a daily basis. When I spoke about the defence by the police, I was referring to some exceptional situations when an area was in danger. When the lines were weak, when there was the threat of enemy piercing our lines, then the army, if they were not able to repel such an attack on their own, they would call the police. However, our daily, regular forces carrying out the daily police work, they didn't go there as often. They would be helped by two or three members of the special unit, because they were the only ones who were able to handle anti-armour weapons in order to stop an attack or any similar vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was it members of the special unit of the regular police who would engage in these fighting activities in support of the army?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: And in certain cases, intervention platoons belonging to the police stations which were closest to the area in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did the special unit have a name?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: It was commonly referred to as Bosna, although we always called them the specials. They were the only members of the special force that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was there a unit that had the name Lasta?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know when exactly that was. Maybe in 1993. But our centre of the Security Service set up a kind of intervention unit which was called that way, that is, the Lasta Special Unit. Their members were police officers from the police stations in the area, and the more competent police officers became members of this special police unit, Lasta. And it was under the control of the Sarajevo centre of the Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did members of Lasta have a special uniform?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: That's right. They had black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What about members of Bosna? Did they have a special uniform?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Well, they wore all sorts of things, as far as I could see. I'd say that the olive-green/grey prevailed, but at times they had camouflage uniforms. They wore all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did the police, that is, the regular members of the police service, ever become involved in the fighting other than in a responsive fashion, that is, other than in response to an attack from the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: No, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: During the armed conflict, did you investigate only offences where civilians were the victim, or did you sometimes investigate offences where members of the military were victims?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: My job as a CI inspector was in addition to my regular activities in the CID also included inspections, investigations on site, the filing of records of events, but only fatalities, fatalities in civilian areas, which means that it was the civilians who were, by and large, the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will take you now to some particular investigations in which you were involved. The first such investigation relates to an incident which occurred on the 22nd of July, 1994. Do you remember investigating an incident on that date?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How did you come to know of an incident on that date? How did you first become aware of it?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Well, I can give you a general question. How I learnt it that day, I don't know, but the rule was that the operations officer, the duty officer, would receive information and then report to the duty inspector. So that is how the information was forwarded and how we received it. So unless it was a specific case, and in that case I would have learned about it in a car, by radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P2790. There is an English translation, which is .1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you assist Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber and my learned colleagues, the evidence of this incident relates to scheduled sniping incident number 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document that you have been handed?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Sorry. Let me see. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is that an official note made by you on the 22nd of July, 1994?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: For the transcript, we have on the ELMO at the moment the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In that note, do you say that at 5.00 on that date, you received a message by radio of two persons being wounded and one killed?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you immediately attend the Novo Sarajevo police station to make some further inquiries in relation to those casualties?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes, quite. Quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How many separate incidents were involved with those three casualties, that is, the two persons wounded and one killed?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Did you attend a scene following your inquiries at the police station?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And whereabouts did you go to? What street?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: In the police station, I received the information that a person had been killed, and that is why I organised the investigation. However, when I arrived in Miljenka Cvitkovica Street in the Novo Sarajevo municipality, that is when I got to the scene, I learned that a child had been wounded by a bullet from a firearm, and it was then that I organised the investigation on site, but I turned over the direct responsibility to the police station of Novo Sarajevo, even though I was present at the on-site investigation, and that is why I wrote this official note.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Whilst you were at the scene, did you view any damage made by small rounds, bullets?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, next to the scene of the incident, there is a catering outlet, and in its window shop and inside, one could clearly see the traces of bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you speak to any eyewitnesses of the incident?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes. In this catering outlet, there were witnesses, and we conducted interviews with them so as to acquire a complete picture about the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was the child still at the scene when you arrived, that is, the child who had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: No. The child had already been taken to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You understand that the child was a boy by the name of Seid Solak?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You've referred to a food outlet. Do you mean by that a restaurant?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Well, something of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Whilst you were there, did you see photographs taken of the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes. I helped, since I was a more experienced officer, so I instructed them how to document everything related to the incident as best as possible. So I saw those photographs and I saw how they recorded the trajectory of the bullets, and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Whilst you were there, did you see members of UNPROFOR apparently carrying out an investigation with members of the police force?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you understand from speaking to eyewitnesses that apparently two shots had been fired, the second shot immediately after the first?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was it pointed out to you where the boy had been standing at the time that he was shot?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you discover in relation -- I withdraw that. And was that outside the restaurant and a short distance from it, that is, from the entrance?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes, outside the restaurant, next to a passage through the building next to the entrance into the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the shot that entered the restaurant, were you able to discover more than one impact point made by the bullet?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes. There were three.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the -- having regard to the trajectory of the bullet, what was the first impact point? In other words, what did it first go through?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: In front of this catering outlet was a canvas, an awning, on a metal frame, and the bullet went through the canvas, which was plastified. I hope you understand what I'm talking about. It was an awning, plastic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The second was in the glass, in the window shop of the facility, and the third one was in the wall, in the interior of the facility, outlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was any attempt made to connect the holes made by the bullet in order to establish a line of sight to the direction from which it came?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was any particular instrument used in that exercise?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was that instrument?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Well, the simplest way to do it, and perhaps I forgot to mention it, but if you have two points, one behind the other, then one can take a simple hollow tube, a small pipe, and if you put -- depending of course on the width of the opening. However, so that is the simplest way. However, that day we used a device which was designed by Borislav Stanko, who is a prominent ballistics expert, and who developed an appliance which is like a periscope but displays horizontally, and it had a kind of antenna because -- and it could go even through the smallest openings. And there was this part with a lens to view it. And if you looked through this -- at this periscope, you could establish the exact place where the bullet had been fired from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know whether that device took into account that the trajectory of a bullet is not precisely a straight line?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: In that particular case, it was obvious --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We could not hear the end of the witness's answer. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you mind repeating that answer. We did not hear all of your words.

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: In this -- in this particular case, since the bullet went through the canvas very easily and hit the glass, one could establish easily that it was a straight line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you visually connected those first two impact points, what did you see at the end of that line?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: When we did what you just said, we saw a house which was well known in that part of the city as the Przulj house. Perhaps there were several houses known by the same surname. But that was an ill-famed house, a notorious house, and I knew about this Przulj house for a long time. But that day we could establish easily that the bullet came from that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On what street was that house?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: From what I knew about Sarajevo, it was Zagorska Street. However, you realise we could not go to the scene to exactly establish -- to identify the street. But from what I know about Sarajevo and its streets and from interviews with witnesses, the name of the street is Zagorska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In what municipality was that street?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Novo Sarajevo, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On what side of the confrontation line, on that date, was that street?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: On the side of the army of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P2792. I have no further questions in relation to Exhibit P2790.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would that please be returned to the registrar. Yes. And could you, Mr. Usher, provide the witness with the document requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could the document first be shown to the witness and then placed on the ELMO. Perhaps the cover could be first placed on the ELMO. To avoid reflection, perhaps the paper could be placed upwards rather than the clear plastic sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the folder as being a photo file in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Indeed, do you recognise the photos in it as having been taken on the day of the incident, in your presence, that is, the 22nd of July, 1994? I should say the photographs of the scene of the crime.

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps the Court usher could turn to the first page, ending with ERN number 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is that a view of the outside of the food outlet or catering outlet or restaurant?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please turn to the next page, which, amongst other numbers, has an ERN number ending in 67. Does that photograph show where you understand the victim was when he was wounded by sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: According to the caption, it was near a shoe store. Does that accord with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What is the fluid which appears on the footpath to the left of centre in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Blood, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please go to the next photograph, which shows a boy lying in bed with a large bandage area in the lower abdomen. Do you understand that to be a photograph of the victim?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: For the transcript, that was the ERN number ending in 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please now go to the next photograph, ending in number 69. Does that show the first impact point of the bullet being on the sunshade outside the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And so as to be clear on this, we're not talking about the bullet that wounded the boy, but the second bullet that was fired immediately after, which penetrated the nearby restaurant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please go to the next photograph, which ends in numbers 70. Does that show the second impact point being the glass at the front of the cafe or restaurant?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please go to the next photograph, which is 71. Do you know the identity of the person who appears in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: No, I don't. It's a visitor who was in this outlet when it happened, but I believe that the members of the Novo Sarajevo police station identified the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is he pointing to the third impact point, that is, the wall, where the bullet ended up?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please go to the next photograph, which ends in numbers 72. Does that show, as you understand it, the bullet which ended up on the cafe floor?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes, that is the bullet that was found in the outlet when it ended its path.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What size is the bullet?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: It is 7.62, a rifle bullet. I'm not a ballistics expert, but I'm talking on the basis of my previous experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And finally, shall we go to photograph 73. Is that a photograph taken on that date --

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- showing the general direction from which you concluded the bullet came?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes. It was at my insistence, even though that is a technical job. But after it was established that it had come from this direction, then they took a shot of this area, and that is the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you see in that photograph the approximate position of the house that you referred to as being the established source of fire?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it is the roof above a white building that you can see below this rim which is encircled, and I think it is, as far as I know, as far as I can recall, that should be the house from which the fire came.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might that be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, I wish to ask you some questions about some other incidents which you investigated. Do you recall investigating an incident which occurred on the 9th of November, 1993 involving the shelling of a school?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Whereabouts was the school?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: It was I think the worst case that I had during these four years of war. That school, it was a provisional class which was temporarily accommodated in a building on Zavnobih Square, that's its old name, and the locality is Alipasino Polje. And that particular class had just one room. There were pupils there, and it was protected with vertical concrete slabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P1840. There is an English translation, .1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please assist Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Kucanin, do you have before you a 3-page report, together with a cover sheet, being a report signed by you at the bottom of page 3?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is this a report made by you on the following date, that is, the 10th of November, 1993, in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes. I drew up this record on the scene of the crime, so I did it there on the spot. It was simply typed out on the 10th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't propose to take you through the detail of this incident, since we have your report to read, but I will ask you some questions in relation to it. First of all, how many shells were fired -- I withdraw that. How many shells impacted on or near the school?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: There was a shell that landed right next to the school building. It killed and wounded several individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What size was -- first of all, what type of shell was it? Was it an artillery shell, tank shell, mortar shell, or what?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: It was a mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What size was the mortar shell?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was a 120-millimetre shell, but that information should be in the report. But off the top of my head, I think it was a 120-millimetre shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please look at your report, in particular, I think, at page 2, about a third of the way down, in the second -- the last line of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, am I right in understanding what you refer to as page 2 is the second page of the report itself, but numbered 3 at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in fact, I should have clarified that. I'm referring to the Bosnian version of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On the English version, the relevant place is page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just past halfway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I refer you to page 2 of your report, that is, the Bosnian-language version. On that page, at the end of the second paragraph, did you refer to the calibre of the mortar shell?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes. It was a 120-millimetre-calibre shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, how many people were killed by the impact of that mortar shell?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: This mortar shell killed the teacher, the lady teacher, whose name was Fatima Gunic and three pupils, one was 6 and two were 9 years old. So four individuals were killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How many people were injured by the shell impact?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: 21, mostly children.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the witness be shown a map, the standard Prosecution map. I think it's Exhibit P3644, and it would be MK1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. I don't know whether it is this map which is almost completely covered in red, and we cannot make it out any more. I say this because there are so many premarked things. If this is the map we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the Defence should like to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have some additional copies. Might that map be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Kucanin, could you please look at the map, take your time, and if you can find it, could you use the pointer to show us where the school was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps the camera could zoom back so we can place this part of the map in context. I think we can see the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you see the position of the school?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes, though I'm not an expert, and I apologise. There are no inscriptions here, and I don't have my glasses with me. But in my opinion, in my estimate, the location would be here, more or less, in this part of the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you have your glasses nearby?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: I left them in the witness room.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps we might come back to that after the morning break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So for the moment, perhaps the map could be taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And perhaps you could retrieve your glasses during the morning break. Was there another incident that day involving a shelling that you investigated?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes, there was. In another part of the same neighbourhood, in another section of the square, another shell landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Approximately how far from the school did that shell land?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Again, it is my estimate that the shell fell some 200 metres away from the school, on Rade Koncara Square. That is the name of the square.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: From the inquiries that you made, did you understand the shells to fall at the same time, a few minutes apart, or hours apart, or what?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but -- I don't think I can tell you the exact time, but one followed the other. The one that landed at the school building was the first one to fall, and then this one came after. You have to bear in mind that, after all, it was all ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I appreciate that. What was the -- first of all, I take it that that second shell was also a mortar shell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the size of the second shell?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: I think it was the same size, 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In what type of area did it land? In other words, was it park land, residential land, industrial land, or what?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: It was a residential area on a square which was covered with concrete blocks, and obviously the objective was to kill as many civilians as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How long before you arrived at the scene did you understand the shell had landed?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Usually we came to the scene not later than one hour after the incident had occurred, so we would always be there at the scene within one hour, although there were certain exceptional cases when, due to constant shelling, we were unable to visit the scene to carry out investigation right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you notice any military equipment nearby when you arrived, such as trucks or weaponry?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you notice any soldiers in the vicinity when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: I didn't notice any particular formation. A citizen in uniform may have passed by, but there was no military formation there. Later on I learned -- but the name escapes me at the moment, but nothing that would indicate that there was any military presence in the area. No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interfere? In the translation it says that later you learned of -- and then you didn't finish that part of your answer. Could you please tell us what you learned later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That there was some kind of headquarters there, perhaps not headquarters, but a logistical base. I don't know what the facility is normally called, when records of -- where records of soldiers are kept. There was some kind of outpost there belonging to a unit, but I don't remember the name of this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How many people were killed, if any, as a result of that shell?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: As far as I recall, three civilians were killed, and the number of wounded was 18, approximately. Later on, no mention was made of that in my report. Several more people died as a result of injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You said that the three killed were civilians. What about the -- sorry. I withdraw that. You said that the three people who in your report were named as killed were civilians. What about the 18 minimum that were -- I withdraw that. What about the people wounded who I think you said was approximately 18 and of whom some later died? Do you know whether they were civilians or military or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: According to what I know, though you were able to see that yourself, in my reports, I usually mention the information about the number of victims, the killed and the wounded, including witnesses as well. And as far as I was aware at that moment, all of them were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time, and I remember you said you wished each side to have five minutes. Would that therefore be a convenient time to suspend examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If this is a convenient moment. You could go on for four or five moments, but if you say this would be a suitable moment, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It would be, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know whether we are going to talk about Rule 90(H). If that is the case, I think that we should do it in writing, in view of the time that it might take. I don't know whether that was the issue that my learned friend, Mr. Ierace, wanted to raise and debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I think when we discussed this issue of Rule 90(H), I don't think that there's any reason why Mr. Kucanin should attend it. Mr. Kucanin, we have a legal, technical issue we'd like to discuss for a couple of minutes before we have a break. It's of no use for you to be present, so I'll ask the usher to lead you out of the courtroom and we'll resume at 11.00. So you're off for 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I would rather wait and see what happens and then decide on whether we need any written exchange of views on Rule 90(H), but I'd like to give the parties both just a couple of minutes in order to -- first of all, to give Mr. Ierace the possibility to explain what he actually seeks, and then for the Defence to respond to that. And this might result in an invitation to the parties to prepare something in writing for the Chamber. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are two points that I wish to make in relation to Rule 90(H)(ii), but before I make those points approximate, I would remind the Trial Chamber and my learned colleagues that on a number of occasions since this trial has commenced, I have drawn the attention of the Trial Chamber to Rule 90(H)(ii). In particular, I have made the point that in the context of the Prosecution case, the Defence is required, by the word "shall," to put its case to the witness if that witness's evidence contradicts the Defence case. I think I'm correct in saying that if it has happened, it's happened perhaps once or twice that it has been put to a witness that their evidence is incorrect. If evidence is inconsistent with a party's case, it seems to me that the witness should be -- it should be put to the witness that either they are being untruthful or they are mistaken, and that has rarely happened, if at all, with any of the witnesses. By now the Prosecution has called approximately 40 witnesses, and we are probably between a quarter and a third of the way through the viva voce evidence in the Prosecution case. Having reminded the Trial Chamber and the Defence of this provision of the Rules, it seems to me that the Prosecution is entitled to conclude that except if the rare circumstance, if at all, where it has been put to a witness that their evidence is incorrect, the Prosecution is entitled to assume that none of the evidence which has been called to date and which has been tendered by the Prosecution is inconsistent with the Defence case. So that is the first point I wish to make. It seems to me that it is appropriate for me to state on the record in the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution takes that view. It could not be said because the Rule has been repeatedly been referred to that there is any misunderstanding on the part of the Defence as to the requirement of that Rule. And again I emphasise the use of the word "shall," not "may." It is a strict requirement. I note that yesterday, in the Milosevic trial, the Trial Chamber, in relation to the accused President Milosevic, did not require him to comply with the Rule, but rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry to interrupt my colleague, but I see the word "shall" in the transcript, which has been translated by the word "shell" or "obus" in French. So I wanted to draw your attention to this particular problem of the French interpretation and the French transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. It has been amended already.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really apologise to my learned friend, Mr. Ierace, but I really thought it was a very essential matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to my friend. Whilst in that trial, as I understand it, the accused is not compelled to comply with this requirement. The Trial Chamber made clear that a relevant factor was that he is unrepresented, and indeed I note in the wording of the Rule that it is counsel who is required to put the contradiction to the witness. In this case, of course, the accused is represented, and in my respectful submission to the Trial Chamber, there can be no reason for the Defence in this trial to not put to each witness what of that witness's evidence is inconsistent, is contradictory to the Defence case. Mr. President, the second point I wish to make goes to the apparent reasoning behind the Rule. What if we arrive at the end of the Prosecution case and enter the Defence case and then the Defence calls evidence which is contradictory to evidence called in the Prosecution case, that evidence might be something said by the accused, for instance, if he gives evidence. It then leaves the Prosecution, and more Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. particularly, you, Mr. President, and Your Honours, with something of a dilemma, because it hadn't been put to the relevant witness or witnesses in the Prosecution case. And had it been put, it may well be that there was a ready answer that the witness or witnesses could have given. The Trial Chamber would then have the dilemma of working out whether witnesses who had been called in the Prosecution case should be recalled. The Prosecution would then have the dilemma of working out whether that was possible and seeking trying to arrange it, and no doubt at great expense. So that is a practical consequence if the Defence is aware of instructions or evidence in its case which it proposes to tender which is contradictory to the evidence given in the Prosecution case. Apart from that practical concern, which could ultimately create problems for the management of this trial, if the Rule is not being applied by the Defence, then we are missing and continue to miss an opportunity to narrow the issues and to save time. Because if ultimately the Defence proposes to contradict some of this material, if we know about it now, then the issues are narrowed and are more apparent. I say "if" for this reason: Since the Defence has been put on notice a number of times about the existence of the Rule, including in the judgement of the Appeal Chamber in December, then one could only assume that, firstly, they are aware of it; and secondly none of the evidence so far called, with perhaps a rare exception, is in contradiction with their instructions. Thank you, Mr. President. Simply, I want to put that on record and point out -- put on record that the Prosecution proposes ultimately to submit that because the Defence has not challenged in a general sense the evidence called, that the Trial Chamber is entitled to conclude that it is not contradicted by the Defence case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, as far as I understand, it's not primarily the scope of the cross-examination, but the application of Rule 90(H)(ii), especially the duty for counsel to put to the witness the nature of the case, in this case, the Defence case. Could you please respond to Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm looking at the clock. Time is fleeing by. I should need a certain amount of time in order to respond. However, let me just say -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may continue. I'll grant you as much time as Mr. Ierace took. That means approximately 11 minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think it would be perhaps better to have a break now, in view of the hour. But let me just say that the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. -- that the Defence makes mention of the fact that the Rule invoked by Mr. Ierace and the problems invoked is in contradiction with Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute, which govern the right to equitable and fair trial, and that this particular provision should be considered, practically speaking, as null and void. That is what we wanted to indicate. And I am -- I think I can say that the Defence counsel in the Talic case and in certain other cases, where there's no Defence such as in the Milosevic case, I think that taking the same position regarding this particular provision. I don't know whether, in view of the hour, you would prefer to proceed with the break. I can elaborate my point. On the other hand, I can perhaps do it in writing, which is a better solution, because we will also be saving time by proceeding that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I, as a matter of fact, am not aware of any case where one of the parties relied on Rules 20 and 21 of the Statute in order to argue that the obligation for counsel to put to the witness the nature of its case was not in conformity with these Articles. This, of course, is different from the general part of the Rule as far as it limits the scope of the cross-examination. So what I suggest to you is that we'll have a break, perhaps a bit shorter than usual, and resume at 10 minutes to 11.00 in order to give you an opportunity to respond specifically on the obligation as stated in Rule 90(H), under (ii), and whenever you'd like to make any submissions as far as the problem of the inconsistency of Rule 90(H) in general with Article 20 and 21 of the Statute of the Tribunal is concerned, I think we could discuss that then later, once we've received your submissions in this respect. So I'd like to split up clearly the obligation of counsel to put to the witness the nature of its case and the general problem you raised is that whether Rule 90(H) violates Article 20 or 21 of the Statute. So on this first issue, you'll have an opportunity in 20 minutes to respond. On the second issue, we'll wait for your written submissions. We'll then adjourn until 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you for giving me the floor. To begin with, so that one the position of the Prosecution, it seems that it is done -- that very indirectly, the Defence is reproached with being the one, if I understood properly what Mr. Ierace said, that we are being reproached with not behaving quite in line, which would seem, and I repeat, which would seem to be required by Rule 90(H)(ii) of the Rules. Now, Mr. President, Your Honours, we have a problem here, which is a fundamental problem. It is a fundamental problem because whatever the manner which one elects -- chooses to examine, we come back always to the same question, to the same question which we have to examine here and now, hic et nunc. Rule 90(H)(ii) was drafted in English in a way and in a different form in French, but one understands what is the general idea behind them. However, what should be examined is what is the source, what is the -- what is behind this provision, and that is -- and in a manner which one might call a theological -- that is, it is in a theological manner to see what was the genesis of this particular provision. And this position precisely, that is, Article -- Rule 90(H)(ii), finds its origins, of course, not in -- obviously in the continental system that we normally apply and which some members of the Chamber know perfectly well, not to say all, but in an Anglo-Saxon system, and in the Anglo-Saxon system, there is a difference, because it seems that the source of this provision is more specifically the British system, that it is a kind of the heritage, of the legacy from the English language, and that means an important consequence for the Chamber. Because in the British criminal system we basically have not a Chamber of professional but a jury, which is made of lay individuals. Now, bearing in mind this detail, Mr. President, and we shall see in a moment, it turns -- it transpires indeed that in the British system there is a difference between this system and other Anglo-Saxon system, it would seem -- and I am speaking very conditionally, because this is not really my area, and I apologise in advance -- but it would seem that to a certain extent, the silence of the accused may be maintained in part or totally, sometimes totally, that it be held against him. On the other hand, in the system of the American time, this silence can in no way, in no way, in the criminal law, may be taken against the accused. What we -- the adage that we all know here is that the one who is silent agrees, is not really accepted in the international jurisdiction, and in no way can we accept that this fundamental principle of the rights of the accused to defend himself by silence, that it be violated in any way. There is a clear decision, both in international law and with regard to this Chamber -- and I apologise if I take five or six minutes more in order to make myself sufficiently clear -- but there are clear decisions which indicate to which extent this right of the Defence, or rather, of the accused, needs to be preserved. I will quote certain things; that is, I will be quoting certain references and you may take note of them. Now, concerning the attitude of the Defence during some of the 40 examinations and cross-examinations which we could now follow, it is quite obvious -- it is obvious that every time the Defence did not say to this or that witness that he was not telling the truth merely for reasons of politeness, which is our natural behaviour, and it is on the other hand up to your Chamber of professionals to see what is the attitude of the witness, what were the difficulties to obtain answers when asked by the Prosecution, and that, esponte sua, the Chamber should have helped the Defence not because the Defence did not have its proper argument, but because I believe one could well see that some of the witnesses were to a certain point reluctant to answer and speak the truth. There was also a witness, and I'm not afraid to say it now before this Chamber, that a witness here gave a false testimony; that is, the witness who first affirmed that his father was not a soldier, whereas effectively, when questioned by the Defence, the witness admitted that the father was a member of the army. Such type of statements -- and you have seen it -- and the Defence tries to apply this approach every time in order to clarify matters. Why, Mr. President, is it not right, is it not possible to ask the Defence, in an imperative manner, that is, to apply the word "shall" to every time produce documents which will challenge the witness's statement? Well, why don't we do it? Well, simply because we can imagine a situation where, for reasons which have to deal strictly with the strategy of the Defence, and that is the absolute right of the accused. One can well imagine that this accused chooses to keep silent so that ultimately, when it comes to his case, to show what was the reality of the things, what was the real state of affairs. It is also quite possible that at that particular moment, that at this particular moment the accused does not have all the elements in his hands to efficiently challenge this or that witness, but that it also presumes that he is not perhaps completely certain and that investigators have to do a number of things so as to come up with their own results. And we, Mr. President, we know that your Chamber is particularly concerned to hear what the witness has to say. I will remind the application of Rule 91 to remind the witness what were the consequences of the lapses of memory, and you will remember that we asked you to do that a number of times because there was a statement which was not correct, and the Chamber said that it would not do that. Well, I took note of that. Now, right. To go back to those indications which I will put to you now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You approximately used your time. You covered a lot of specific subjects. You indicated false testimony in this Court. You spent some time to the right to silence, which I would not say everything, of course, is related to everything, but which was not the specific subject I asked you to respond on. So if you could please conclude in two, not more than three minutes, specifically on the subject I asked you to respond on, your observation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. President. The decision which I will quote now are the following: You have the Delalic case, and I would suggest that you read paragraph 58. I believe that the case is well known. But I will also give you the references in a moment, if you wish me to do so. I will find it in a moment. I'm sorry. I was interrupted, so ... But here we have the Delalic case, number of the Delalic case, and then you have paragraph 58, and there is an interesting quote which says.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking the counsel to put it on the ELMO for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put the part you're quoting on the ELMO so that the interpreters will be able to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you want me to, yes, I shall be happy to do so, but to gain time, it suffices merely to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it's the wish of the interpreters, who are trying to do their job as good as they can, which I follow at this moment. Of course, it will not be deducted from your three minutes. Please, would you -- do you have a copy or ... otherwise quote --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will take me several minutes to prepare that. You are asking too much of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I'm just asking you whether there's a copy. I'm not blaming you. I'm trying to find a solution for those professionals in the booth who have to perform their duties. That's what I'm trying to solve, and nothing else. So would you -- if you have no copy, then please read it slowly. If you have a copy, please put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do not have any other copy. I didn't have any time to copy during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you then please read slowly the part of the Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber, in the Delalic case, paragraph 58, says as follows, and I'm quoting: "[In English] It is the sacred and solemn duty of every judicial institution to respect and give construction to the provisions granting such right instead of giving such a construction as to whittle down their effect." [Interpretation] You will find this in the Delalic case. There are also obviously other decisions on the international scale, and I can quote for the Chamber the decision which comes from the American law, which says the same thing, and that is Miranda versus Arizona case, that is 384 US 436460 of 1966 and it is a decision where it is again -- where there is again mentioned the inviolable character of the defendant to remain silent. And if I say this, it is because there is quite a number of things related to Rule 90(H)(ii) where this right to remain silent may be violated if we every time have to do what the Prosecution wants us to do. Mr. President, I believe that these decisions, that is, the Delalic decision which with I have just quoted, that is, the 58th paragraph of it, are sufficiently clear and they allow you to reach a decision on this point. I'm sorry if I took ten minutes more from the time that was assigned to me, but I believe I used properly these ten minutes. Thank you very much. And I'm sorry that I had to take more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for just a couple of minutes in order to give a response to the observation of Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Ierace, is there anything you would like to add at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps if I just speak for two minutes or so in response, or would you prefer I didn't?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Very briefly, it has nothing to do with the accused's right to silence; it's to do with fairness. And there are some efficiency gains if the Rule is complied with. Secondly, it is not for the Defence or the Prosecution, for that matter, to ignore the Rules. We are obliged to follow them. Thirdly, I note that my friend has still not said whether or not they are complying with the Rule. He said these words: "Why don't we do it? Well, simply because we can imagine a situation where, for reasons which have to deal strictly with the strategy of the Defence, and that is the absolute right of the Defence." And finally, he refers to practical problems which the Defence would have in complying with the Rule, where further investigation work is required to be undertaken by the Defence investigators. Mr. President, I quite agree. I can well imagine that many of the aspects of evidence which emerge in the Prosecution case require some further investigation before the accused could place his position on the record. Therefore, my approach is that whilst there are some occasions when one could not expect reasonably the accused, through his counsel, to challenge evidence at this stage, that does not explain a total inadequacy to do so if indeed the evidence is contrary to his instructions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, another two minutes for you if you are in need -- if you feel any need to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. No, we shall retain theses two minutes, and we believe that this provision needs to be considered as nil unless the Prosecution tries every time to follow a procedure which is just as fair and unbiased as possible. To bear in mind -- because in other cases, otherwise it would be considered as a flagrant violation of Articles 20 and 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. We'll then adjourn for just a couple of minutes. So many minutes as we need. So I can't give you an exact time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered what has been said by Mr. Ierace and Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The Chamber will be glad to receive submissions on the issue, as indicated by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, so that the Prosecution could respond to that in writing as well. On the basis of the views expressed until now, the Chamber finds no reason not to apply Rule 90(H), and more specifically, 90(H)(ii). The Chamber stresses that, in its view, as it is at this moment, Rule 90(H) does not prevent the Defence from presenting whatever evidence they might find in a later stage during their investigations when the Defence is presenting its case. So those are our decisions for the time being. I do think, Mr. Ierace, we are at the point where we could resume the examination of Mr. Kucanin, as I hope, with glasses. And I'll just use the time available in order to inform everyone in this courtroom that since the first break was a bit shorter, we'll have the long break as the second break. That's my first remark. The second one is that I indicate to the parties that on the 6th of March we'll not hear the case as usually in the morning, but in the late afternoon session. That would mean from a quarter past 2.00 until 7.00. I think it's Wednesday, the 6th of March. Mr. Kucanin, please be seated. I know that you had to wait already last week for quite some time and now it's even one half of an hour extra. We apologise for that. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I ask that the witness be shown again the map. That's Exhibit P3644 MK1.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Kucanin, you told us about two shelling incidents that you investigated on the 9th of November, 1993, and you've told us that as a result of inquiries that you made, they happened at about the same time. The school incident happened first and the second shell that landed about 200 metres away immediately followed. Are you able to find on the map, now that you are wearing your glasses, the site of the school?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: As I have already indicated, the location was a residential block. The ground floor of that residential block was turned into a school, so we cannot call it actually a school. It was not a school building. It's just that during that period of time it housed one classroom which was used as a school. And as I indicated earlier on, this was on Zavnobih Square.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you please take a blue marker pen and place a cross over the position of the classroom which was used as a school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please leave it on the ELMO, Mr. Kucanin. Perhaps the ELMO could be moved so that we can see how you -- yes, that's visible now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please place the number 1 alongside the cross.

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did your investigation team include a ballistics expert?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did the investigation establish, firstly, the direction of the trajectory of the mortar shell?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was that direction?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: From this point in time, all I can tell you is that it was told that it had come from the direction of Nedzarici, which at the time was occupied by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you see on the map the area of Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Indeed, I think on the map we can see the name Nedzarici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Are you able to identify on the map the part of Nedzarici which was under the control of the Bosnian Serb army on that date?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: I think this lower part of the neighbourhood, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you place a circle or -- I withdraw that. Would you draw a -- I withdraw that. Do you know approximately the position of the confrontation line in the Nedzarici area on that date?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Approximately. I know because my brother lived in this building here that I'm indicating now, which was on this side of the street, on our side. So the line, I think, was along this line here, more or less. But I'm by no means an expert for maps or a military expert. I know that it was not possible to walk along this street, because this area here was directly exposed to sniper fire. A military barracks was here, which had remained in the hands of Bosnian Serbs. So that is why soldiers were quartered here, and fire was opened from this location, as we could hear from the witnesses who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: For the benefit of the transcript, you referred to a number of places in your last answer. You referred to the place of residence of your brother, which was approximately above the name Mojmilo, which appears on the map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: Yes. In the Mojmilo neighbourhood, that is where my brother lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And you've indicated approximately the position of part of the front line. I appreciate that you don't know exactly where it was. Where that understanding, would you please take the blue marker pen and, to the best of your understanding, place the approximate position of the front line in the Nedzarici region.

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the benefit of the record, you've placed a line to the right and above the name Nedzarici. Now, assuming that the top of the map is north, it would therefore seem that the direction of fire was to the south-west; is that correct, that is, to the south-west of the school, or the classroom?

utterances.speaker: Mirsad Kucanin
utterances.text: As I told you, I'm not an expert, but if I had put down the direction in my report, that should be taken into account. That is, if the ballistics experts had given me the right direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In any event, did you understand from the ballistics experts that the source of fire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. I have to intervene once again for the benefit of the transcript. The French booth has invented an answer of the witness, line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- 45 or 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpretation is the interpreters invented an answer of the witness. Would you please indicate if there's any mistake in view of you, in the translation, would you refrain from using words like "inventions." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a posteriori, with hindsight, it is an invention, to the extent that Mr. Ierace said, for the record, he was going to explain what has happened, that is, what the witness has indicated on the map, which line and where. He did that for the benefit of the record. After that, the French booth invented an answer of the witness, which was "yes." If I cannot speak here, as counsel of General Galic, I will keep quiet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it's just a matter of the words you're using. If you say that something was translated what was not said, the word "inventing" has a specific meaning, and I think it's unfair to the interpreters to use it, and I'll allow you, as you know, to make whatever comment on any mistake in the translation or anything translated which, in your view, has not been said. As a matter of fact, it's my recollection that the witness did give a very short word at that moment, but let's -- if you want to listen to the tape, it's fine. But I'd just like to keep the tone of our discussions as neutral as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
